<reason>Both sides argued competently on the real clash (does the debt stock or the productivity of new spending decide the question), but A controlled the decisive exchanges. A's dismantling of CON's WWII analogy (primary surpluses from demobilization, favorable demographics, financial repression, r below g) was specific and mechanism-level, and B's reply — that the "mechanism" of growth-driven denominator expansion is unaffected by those disanalogies — largely restated the claim rather than defending it. A also neutralized the Eurozone comparison by distinguishing consolidation at full employment from cutting into a depression, and B's rejoinder ("if it backfires under stress it backfires under calm too") was an unsupported inference rather than an answer. Most importantly, B's strongest attack — that PRO's "high-return investment can clear a higher bar" escape hatch swallows "most" new commitments — was answered cleanly and originally by A's reframe that the bar is *financing*, not category: an offset-funded grid upgrade passes, the same upgrade on a permanent deficit does not. That made A's rule genuinely binding against its own preferences, and B never dislodged it. B's late attempt to define expiring tax cuts, benefit expansions and defense plus-ups as "legacy law" rather than new commitments overreached and was punished in A's closing without reply. B's refusal to name any threshold was defensible in principle (r versus g rather than a cliff), but B never argued that its own dynamic test currently passes, leaving A's "your rule can never say no" framing live through the ballot. B's closing reframe to "what actually shrinks the ratio" is a fair metric dispute and its productive-versus-consumption distinction retains some force, but B's claim that A "never rebutted it, not once" is inaccurate given the paid-for reframe. A's two clipped turns are a real execution cost, and B's Q1 answer (share of new commitments that pay for themselves) was partly dodged; net, A wins clearly but not dominantly.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's response to the "escape hatch" charge: recasting the higher bar as a financing test rather than a category test ("a grid upgrade with an offset passes; the same upgrade bolted onto a permanent deficit does not"), which restored the bite of "most new commitments" and forced B into the overreaching "legacy law" carve-out that A punished unanswered in closing.</best_rebuttal>
